headline: A weak 10 year auction pushed yields to about 5% and Nvidia fell another 5.5%, but CoreWeave's beat and raise has Nasdaq futures up about 1.9% this morning; no put passes the screen today.
summary: Prices are Tuesday Nov 10 closes from Massive. The dashboard is a day behind (prices_as_of 2026-11-09; the Nov 10 close is missing and no Massive fill ran), so its verdicts and zones are from Nov 9. Tuesday: the Treasury sold $42 billion of 10 year notes at 5.02%, 1 basis point over the pre sale yield, with weaker demand (bid to cover 2.46 versus 2.77). Futures put a December hike near 90% and a half point near 10% (CNBC; Benzinga). NVDA fell 5.47% to 168.89 as the probe reports grew, and QQQ slipped 0.68% to 674.76, 1.30% under its 683.69 line. After the close CoreWeave beat and raised its 2026 outlook; it traded up about 15% before the open and Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 1.9% near 8:50am ET (CNBC). Bonds are closed today for Veterans Day. The put screen finds nothing: APH's put went thin, so the idea is dropped.

The offset is real AI demand: CoreWeave's revenue rose 168% and its customers prepaid about $9 billion. signals.title: The 10 year auction tailed and yields sit near 5%; a December hike is close to priced
signals.since_yesterday: The auction result: $42 billion sold at 5.02%, 1 basis point over the pre sale yield, with the bid to cover down to 2.46 from 2.77.
signals.what_happened: Treasury sold $42 billion of 10 year notes at a high yield of 5.02% on Nov 10, against a 5.010% when issued yield, a 1 basis point tail. The bid to cover fell to 2.46 from 2.77 in October (Bloomingbit; RTTNews). The 10 year traded just over 5% during the day (Barchart, 5.01%), and the 2 year rose about 17 basis points to 4.73% (CryptoTicker). After CPI, futures priced a December hike at about 90% and a half point at about 10% (CNBC and Benzinga citing CME FedWatch). UBS expects 25 basis points in December and again in March and calls support for 50 limited (CNBC). Bonds are closed today.
signals.so_what: A tail is small, but it came the same day as a hot print, so buyers asked for more yield to take the supply. Second order: a 5% 10 year raises the bar for every put idea and every dividend stock, and it makes the most expensive growth names work harder. Third order: the $25 billion 30 year sale Thursday is the next test, and a second weak auction would say the problem is supply and not just inflation. What would make this wrong: Fed leaders other than Waller pushing back on 50, or a soft PPI.
signals.for_you: Puts: the bar is now about 5.0% a year; several buy zone premiums no longer clear it once you account for thin trading. Long term: AEP is the buy zone name most exposed to yields, and it closed 3 cents over its zone top. Swing: no change; no setups.

signals.title: CoreWeave beats and raises, and its customers are paying ahead
signals.since_yesterday: The report is out: Q3 revenue $3.66 billion, up 168%, above the $3.55 billion forecast, and the 2026 outlook was raised.
signals.what_happened: CoreWeave's Q3 revenue was $3.661 billion, up 168% from a year ago (company release). LSEG's forecast was $3.55 billion (CNBC). It raised 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 to $13.3 billion from $12.4 to $13.2 billion, and adjusted operating income to $1.275 to $1.375 billion; 2026 capital spending is $37 to $39 billion and fourth quarter interest is guided at $1.05 to $1.15 billion (StockTitan, from the outlook slides). Q3 interest expense was $846 million and the net loss $709 million. Contracted power rose past 4.6 GW. The CEO said about $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits help fund the build. CRWV closed 48.73 on Nov 10, down 0.51% on 90.3 million shares (Massive), and traded at 55.85, up 14.6%, at 8:53am ET (CNBC). Nebius was up 11.4% and IREN 7.9% before the open (CNBC). The release also names a collaboration with Leidos on secure AI cloud work for defense and intelligence.
signals.so_what: This answers the question that hit AI stocks last week: are the buyers still paying? Yes, and some pay in advance. Second order: prepayments and contract backed loans mean the customers, not just lenders, carry part of the build risk, which supports Nvidia, power and cooling suppliers. Third order: the cost is debt. Interest now eats most of operating income, so CoreWeave needs rates to stop rising. A 5% 10 year is the risk to this story. What would make this wrong: Cisco and Applied Materials on Thursday guiding down.
signals.for_you: Swing: CRWV is not on the dashboard as a setup and its verdict is 'Not enough data'; do not chase a 15% gap. Long term: the read across helps APH (still in its zone at 79.95). Puts: no change. LDOS gets a small new AI customer link, but no LDOS put passes on liquidity.

signals.title: Nvidia falls 5.5% more as the probe widens; it bounces before the open
signals.since_yesterday: Two new reports on Nov 10: a US official briefed the President on the CEO's relationship, and the Commerce Department delayed adding Megaspeed to its trade blacklist.
signals.what_happened: NVDA closed 168.89 on Nov 10, down 5.47%, on 429.3 million shares, after a 4.3% fall Monday (Massive). Reports on Nov 10 said Secretary of State Rubio had briefed President Trump on the CEO's relationship with a Megaspeed executive, and the Financial Times said several agencies pushed to put Megaspeed on the entity list while Commerce delayed it (Straits Times summary). The FBI is separately looking at whether the CEO was a target of foreign intelligence (Straits Times). The New York Times reported Nov 9 that the Justice Department took over the Megaspeed probe (CFR summary). Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe security or company secrets were compromised. NVDA was up about 5% before the open (CNBC).
signals.so_what: Every new report so far adds a government body, not a finding. That keeps the risk open until Nvidia reports on Nov 17. Second order: if Megaspeed lands on the entity list, Southeast Asian cloud sales get harder to book, and rivals with less China exposure look safer. Third order: CoreWeave's beat shows the demand side is fine, so this is a governance and export story, not a demand story. What would make this wrong: the board's review clearing the CEO quickly.
signals.for_you: NVDA stays 'Wait' (zone 198.22 to 225.57 from the Nov 9 build, far above the price). No NVDA trade or put before Nov 17. A 5% bounce after two heavy volume down days is not a base.

signals.title: Anthropic IPO: pricing expected Nov 18, first trade Nov 19, valued near $1.4 trillion
signals.since_yesterday: A date: people familiar told CNBC trading should start Nov 19, with pricing expected the night before. Several outlets put the value near $1.4 trillion, not the $1.02 trillion in yesterday's brief.
signals.what_happened: Anthropic is selling 825 million shares at $70 to $78. TechCrunch and Bloomberg put the implied value at $1.404 trillion at the top of the range; yesterday's brief used about $1.02 trillion, which appears to count fewer shares, so we use the $1.4 trillion figure that most outlets report. Trading is expected Nov 19 (CNBC, sources) or Nov 20 (Wall Street Journal via Yahoo); the earliest pricing date is Nov 13 (Yahoo). Each of the 7 founders will sell about $250 million (TechCrunch). The Australian retail book opened Nov 11 and closes Nov 17 at 5pm Sydney time, about 1am ET (CNBC). TSMC's board approved up to $500 million of Anthropic shares at the IPO price and up to $500 million of OpenAI preferred stock (TSMC).
signals.so_what: A $64 billion share sale pulls cash from other AI holdings the week of Nvidia's report. Second order: chip and cloud suppliers that buy in the placement are tying their sales to a customer's share price. Third order: if it prices at the top and trades up, it resets what the market pays for AI revenue, which helps the whole group; a weak debut would hit the same names. Who wins is unclear until it prices, so no tickers are tagged.
signals.for_you: No action. Expect AI names to stay jumpy through Nov 19. Keep any new AI swing small until both Nvidia (Nov 17) and the debut are behind us.

signals.title: Oil: Brent settled at $91.49, not under $90; Iran talk keeps a floor
signals.since_yesterday: Brent dipped under $90 only intraday on Nov 10 and settled at $91.49; it rose 1.4% this morning after Iran said enriched material will not leave the country.
signals.what_happened: Brent settled at $91.49 on Nov 10, down 1.17%, after trading under $90 during the day (NDTV Profit). This morning it was $92.81, up 1.4%, at 8:14am ET, and WTI $87.12 (Reuters). Iran's security chief said Tehran will not let enriched nuclear material leave the country. 37 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October, the most since the war began, and two tankers hit mines this week. US crude stocks rose 9 million barrels last week (API). Brent is down about 21% this month (Reuters).
signals.so_what: Correction to yesterday's brief: 'under $90' was an intraday level, not a close. The big drop this month is about truce hopes; the attacks at sea have not stopped, so the floor holds near $90 for now. Second order: lower oil helps the inflation numbers in a few months, which is the main hope against more Fed hikes. Third order: if a deal ends the Hormuz risk premium (Waller put it at $20 to $30), oil could fall a lot further, which would hurt energy producers and help airlines and consumers.
signals.for_you: No action. No energy setups or energy puts. Oil is the one force that could cool inflation before the Fed's Dec 9 meeting.

Nuclear small caps: cash rich, revenue poor; deals, not quarters, will move them.
signals.for_you: HIMS stays 'Wait' on the dashboard; no puts on a stock falling this hard. FRVO, OKLO and SMR are not on any buy list. RKLB is 'Avoid' on valuation despite the volume.

cycle.big_cycle: Technology and external order are now tangled: the Nvidia probe is about chips reaching China through Singapore, and the Commerce Department is weighing a blacklist (FT via Straits Times). Debt and money: Treasury supply meets weaker demand. Internal order: unchanged since the Nov 3 vote.

history.when: May 16, 2000: the Fed's last half point hike of that cycle
history.what: The Fed raised its target 50 basis points to 6.5% while AI's equivalent then, the internet build, was still spending heavily (Federal Reserve press release).
history.lesson: Big spending on a new technology does not stop the Fed when inflation is the problem. The stocks most dependent on cheap money fell first; the builders with real cash flow held up longer.

history.when: February 1994 to February 1995: the Fed's surprise tightening
history.what: The Fed doubled its target from 3% to 6% in a year and US bond losses reached about $600 billion by late 1994 (Fortune).
history.lesson: Weak auctions and rising long yields came before the stock pain, not after. Watch Thursday's 30 year sale.

cycle.differences: In 2000 the Fed was near the end of its hikes at 6.5%; today it is just starting a new round from 3.75% to 4.00% while the 10 year is already near 5%. And unlike 2000, today's big AI spenders are booking real revenue and prepayments, not just ad money.
